name: Ceasg
description: A mermaid figure of Scottish Gaelic folklore: the upper body of a woman joined to the tail of a grilse (young salmon). Captured ceasgs are said to grant three wishes in exchange for their freedom.
full_description: The ceasg is a mermaid-like creature of Scottish Gaelic Highland and Hebridean folklore. She has the upper body of a beautiful young woman joined to the tail of a grilse (a young salmon), and inhabits both salt water and the rivers and streams that the salmon ascends. Tradition holds that a fisherman who captures a ceasg without injuring her will be granted three wishes for her release. In some stories ceasgs marry mortal men and bear children; several Highland sea-pilots and seafaring families are traditionally said to descend from such unions, and the ceasg-ancestress is sometimes believed to protect her descendants at sea. Other tales are less benign — one widely retold story has a ceasg swallow a hero who survives within her until charmed forth by harp music. The folklorist Donald A. Mackenzie suggested that the ceasg may preserve a memory of an older sea-goddess to whom human sacrifices were offered. The figure is recorded in 19th- and early-20th-century Scottish Gaelic folklore collections, including those of John Gregorson Campbell.
origin: Coastal and riverine Scottish Gàidhealtachd (Highlands and Western Isles).

etymology.origin: Scottish Gaelic ceasg, used in Highland tradition for this mermaid figure.
etymology.meaning: The Gaelic word ceasg refers to the mermaid figure; the descriptive epithets maighdean na tuinne and maighdean mhara mean 'maid of the wave' and 'maid of the sea' respectively.
etymology.first_use: Recorded in Scottish Gaelic oral tradition; published English-language attestations from the 19th century.

timeline.event: John Gregorson Campbell, Superstitions of the Highlands and Islands of Scotland published posthumously, including ceasg material
timeline.significance: Major published source of Highland marine folklore

timeline.event: Donald A. Mackenzie publishes Scottish Folk-Lore and Folk Life with discussion of the ceasg as a possible memory of an older sea-goddess

related.name: Selkie
related.description: Scottish/Faroese seal-people who can take human form; another shapeshifting marine being of Gaelic and Norse-Gaelic tradition

cultural_notes: Traditionally regarded as a real, if rarely encountered, denizen of Highland waters; capturing one without harm is the necessary condition for the bargain.

sources.title: Superstitions of the Highlands and Islands of Scotland
